questions.q: According to ISO 31000, how is risk formally defined?
options: The effect of uncertainty on objectives
The dollar cost of the worst-case scenario a company can imagine
The number of open findings on a risk register
A fixed probability published by a regulator for every threat type
questions.explain: ISO 31000 defines risk as "the effect of uncertainty on objectives." Likelihood × Impact is the practical shorthand most security teams use to operationalize that abstract definition.

questions.q: What is the main reason security teams still use a Likelihood × Impact / 5×5 matrix despite its flaws?
options: It produces legally binding dollar figures for insurance claims
It is fast and requires no statistics background, letting a committee triage many findings quickly
It eliminates the need for any risk register
Regulators require every organization to use exactly this formula
questions.explain: The equation and matrix exist to let a risk committee rank a large pile of findings quickly and defensibly — a triage tool, not a precision financial model.

questions.q: Why does scoring "Impact" as a single number (like 4 out of 5) understate the real risk of some scenarios?
options: Because impact scores are always set by auditors instead of security staff
Because ISO 31000 forbids numeric impact scoring
Because it flattens a range of possible loss outcomes into one point estimate, hiding long-tail catastrophic cases
Because impact can only be measured after a breach has already occurred
questions.explain: Real-world loss is a distribution, not a point. A single impact score can make a tight, predictable medium-impact risk look identical to one with a long tail of rare-but-catastrophic outcomes.

questions.q: What does it mean for two risks on a register to be "correlated," and why does the Likelihood × Impact method typically miss this?
options: It means both risks were discovered on the same audit date, which the matrix already accounts for
It means one risk's score is mathematically derived from the other's score in the matrix formula
It means the two risks cancel each other out and can be removed from the register
It means they share a root cause and may fire — or be remediated — together, but each risk is scored independently of the others
questions.explain: Risks are scored one at a time, but real risks often share a root cause (like a weak identity provider). A single control can retire several register entries at once — something risk-by-risk scoring doesn't reveal.

questions.q: What is the real problem with the Likelihood and Impact inputs that feed the equation, according to this lesson?
options: The multiplication itself is mathematically invalid for security use cases
They are usually soft, consensus-driven estimates, but organizations often treat them as if they were hard measurements
They can only be sourced from a single named industry-wide actuarial table
Impact scores are legally required to come from outside auditors only
questions.explain: Likelihood and Impact are typically informed guesses from whoever is in the risk workshop, not measured frequencies. The equation's math is fine — the failure mode is treating a soft estimate as a hard number.
